newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: No end seen to Uzbek exchange controls, diplomats.
newsitem.headline: No end seen to Uzbek exchange controls, diplomats.

text.p: Uzbekistan is unlikely to scrap foreign exchange controls in the near future despite a visit this week by a senior official from the International Monetary Fund, businessmen and diplomats said on Monday.

The IMF suspended a $185 million loan to the former Soviet republic late last year, criticising the imposition of foreign exchange controls and Uzbekistan's failure to meet the fund's inflation targets.
Last week, Uzbekistan said it had invited the fund's deputy managing director, Stanley Fischer, for talks with President Islam Karimov on Friday to improve relations with the IMF.

Few in the capital Tashkent, however, expect Karimov to give in to fund pressure to lift exchange controls which bedevil foreign investors trying to do business in the largely desert nation of 23 million.
"I'm pessimistic," said a Western diplomat on condition of anonymity. "I don't expect any decision (on lifting exchange controls) during Fischer's visit," he said.
An Uzbek banker concurred. "I do not see any removal of exchange controls," he said. "It would mean a big shock, it would make 70 percent of the population poor overnight," he said.
Desperate for cash to bail out the troubled agriculture sector, the government imposed the exchange controls late last year following disastrous cotton and wheat harvests.

"They're terrified of capital flight and it's unlikely they'll make any changes until the autumn when the results of this year's harvest are clearer," said another Western diplomat, who said cotton accounted for up to 60 percent of the country's export earnings.

The controls have created a flourishing black market in dollars, with the so-called "bazaar rate" at around 145 sums to the dollar, way above the official exchange rate of about 60 sums to the dollar.
The controls have also forced many shops to close and have led to a dearth of goods in those that remain open.
President Karimov has said he aims to make the resource-rich republic a bustling Singapore and the hub of Central Asian business.
But his cautious, go-slow approach to economic reform, with much of the economy still planned, has meant he has been forced to watch neighbouring Kazakhstan forge ahead in this role.

Kazakhstan already boasts foreign debt ratings and has investors flocking to participate in a risky but high-speed privatisation programme. The hustle and bustle of the Kazakh capital Almaty is absent in Tashkent.

Long-term investors, like BAT Industries which plans to invest $300 million in Uzbekistan and which produced five billion cigarettes in the Central Asian republic last year, say they have access to foreign exchange.
"We've been getting convertibility," said Peter Taylor, the chief executive of BAT's Uzbekistan venture. "It's a lengthy process and that gets a bit frustrating," he said.
BAT owns 92 percent of shares in the project, with the remainder held by the government.

But Taylor said investors were overly pessimistic and that Uzbekistan's high level of education and political stability were attractive. "Everyone's sitting on the fence at the moment and waiting to see what happens," he said.
But most businessmen and diplomats say the exchange controls hamper investment.
With few expecting a compromise during Fischer's visit this week, the republic's relations with the IMF look set to remain cool.
